description: I'm Aga, an ML developer from Nigeria and founder of VelkroLM, an AI lab building small models and tools for African languages. We're building FieldShift NG, a tool that turns NASA data into plain-language decisions for Nigerian farmers, from planting to flood risk to when to sell. I'm looking for a frontend developer, a data/GIS person, someone with agriculture knowledge, and a designer. If you're curious and want to build something that matters, join us.
summary:
FieldShift NG is an offline-capable farm decision-support tool designed to help smallholder farmers in northern Nigeria make more informed crop-rotation decisions.
A farmer's planting decision is shaped by more than rainfall. Flood exposure, water availability, soil conditions, storage, previous crops, and market preferences all affect what makes sense to plant. Yet these factors are often considered separately, and useful climate information is not always accessible when connectivity is limited.
FieldShift brings these considerations into one workflow. It processes NASA Earth-observation and climate data into local climate context, combines that context with farmer-provided information, and uses a transparent rule-based engine to compare three-season crop rotations. Farmers can see scores, warnings, alternative plans, and the reasons behind each result.
The platform includes a standard interface and a lightweight version designed for constrained devices, small screens, and feature-phone-oriented use cases.
Rules decide. AI explains. Farmers decide
details:
FieldShift NG — NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 Submission 1. Project Summary FieldShift NG is an offline-capable farm decision-support tool designed to help smallholder farmers in northern Nigeria make more informed crop-rotation decisions. A farmer's planting decision is shaped by more than rainfall. Flood exposure, water availability, soil conditions, storage, previous crops, and market preferences all affect what makes sense to plant. Yet these factors are often considered separately, and useful climate information is not always accessible when connectivity is limited. FieldShift brings these considerations into one workflow. It processes NASA Earth-observation and climate data into local climate context, combines that context with farmer-provided information, and uses a transparent rule-based engine to compare three-season crop rotations. Farmers can see scores, warnings, alternative plans, and the reasons behind each result. The platform includes a standard interface and a lightweight version designed for constrained devices, small screens, and feature-phone-oriented use cases. Rules decide. AI explains. Farmers decide. 2. Project Demonstration Demonstration format: Live application and project presentation. The live application demonstrates the farmer workflow, crop-rotation comparison, decision explanations, and lightweight interface. Standard application: https://fieldshift-ng.vercel.app/ Lite / feature-phone-oriented interface: https://fieldshift-ng.vercel.app/lite.html Source code: https://github.com/rufatronics/fieldshift-ng The presentation or video submitted in this field should demonstrate the problem, the live application, how changing farmer conditions affects the recommendations, and the project's limitations. 3. Project Links Live application: https://fieldshift-ng.vercel.app/ Lite interface: https://fieldshift-ng.vercel.app/lite.html GitHub repository: https://github.com/rufatronics/fieldshift-ng 4. Project Details The problem For a smallholder farmer, choosing what to plant is a connected decision. Rainfall patterns affect crop suitability. Flood-prone land introduces additional risk. Irrigation access changes the options available. Storage conditions influence what can safely be kept after harvest. Previous crops affect the next rotation, while market preferences influence what the farmer wants to grow. These factors are rarely presented together in a simple, understandable decision-support workflow. General weather applications can provide weather information, but they do not necessarily help a farmer compare entire crop rotations under their own conditions. FieldShift NG addresses this gap by turning climate and environmental information into a transparent starting point for farm-planning decisions. How FieldShift works A farmer begins by selecting a language and a broad location zone. The current application includes Kano, Katsina, and Sokoto. The farmer then provides simple information about their field and circumstances: Whether the land is exposed to flooding. Whether irrigation is available. Their storage conditions. Crops planted in previous seasons. Their preferred crops and market priorities. FieldShift combines these inputs with zone-level climate information and evaluates possible three-season crop rotations. It compares the existing rotation with alternative strategies, displays suitability scores and warnings, and explains the factors influencing each result. Farmers can also change scenario assumptions to explore how different conditions affect the comparison. The aim is not to issue an unquestionable planting prescription. It is to make the trade-offs visible so farmers and agricultural extension workers can make better-informed decisions. NASA Earth-observation data FieldShift uses a data-processing pipeline built around four NASA data resources: NASA POWER: Climate variables including precipitation, temperature, humidity, and other environmental indicators. NASA GPM IMERG: Satellite-derived precipitation observations. MODIS NDVI: Vegetation greenness information that provides an additional environmental signal. SRTM: Elevation and terrain information that helps describe local topographic conditions. The pipeline harmonizes data into common 10-day periods, checks data coverage, retains source and unit information, and produces zone-level climate summaries. The current dataset covers three zones—Kano, Katsina, and Sokoto—with climate summaries spanning 2005–2025. These are regional climate summaries, not measurements of conditions on an individual farmer's exact field. FieldShift communicates that distinction rather than presenting regional data as ground truth for a particular farm. The decision engine: Rules decide, AI explains The central decision engine is deterministic and runs in the browser. It evaluates factors including: Water requirements and rainfall availability. Crop duration relative to the growing season. Heat exposure. Flood exposure. Harvest and storage conditions. Soil-related considerations. Crop repetition and rotation sequence. Farmer-selected priorities and preferred crops. The engine applies explicit rules, penalties, bonuses, and safety gates before ranking possible rotations. Optional AI functionality helps explain the engine's results in plain language. It receives structured decision information; it does not determine the scores, remove safety gates, invent agronomic facts, or override farmer inputs. An experimental rainfall-forecasting component can provide additional context. It is advisory, uses a seasonal baseline when the optional model worker is unavailable, and requires further local validation. Forecasts do not control the crop-rotation scoring engine. Accessibility and low-connectivity design FieldShift is designed with the reality of limited connectivity and varied device capabilities in mind. The standard interface provides the full planning experience, including comparisons, visual information, and optional explanations. The Lite interface is a simplified, low-data version designed for smaller screens and constrained browsers. It removes resource-heavy elements and focuses on the essential farm-planning workflow. It is intended to serve feature-phone-oriented use cases, including the familiar keypad-phone environment associated with classic Nokia devices. The project does not assume that every farmer has a modern smartphone or reliable internet access. Its core planning logic is designed to work on the device after the application has been cached. Optional AI explanations require connectivity, and compatibility with individual legacy feature-phone browsers still requires testing. Example: A Kano farming scenario To demonstrate how the decision engine responds to changing conditions, we replayed an illustrative Kano farming scenario. The hypothetical farmer has a low-lying plot, no irrigation, limited storage, and a previous rotation of maize, maize, and groundnut. The scenario applies an illustrative 30% reduction in rainy-season rainfall. Under this tested scenario: The existing rotation receives a score of 65/100. The engine's top alternative, pearl millet → cowpea → sesame, receives 89/100. The alternative performs better under the tested assumptions because of its crop mix, water-related considerations, rotation sequence, and the farmer's stated market preferences. This is an illustrative model replay, not evidence of an observed 2020 drought impact, measured yield improvement, or guaranteed increase in income. The scores are internal suitability scores, not probabilities of success. A heavier flood-stress test also demonstrates why the system needs safety gates: the tested alternative falls to 6/100 and triggers a gate rather than being presented as a safe recommendation. Crop parameters still require validation by agricultural experts before the system can make production-grade recommendations. Creativity and potential impact FieldShift's main contribution is the combination of NASA environmental data, farmer-specific constraints, crop history, and transparent rotation rules in one accessible workflow. Instead of treating satellite data as something that only researchers can interpret, the project attempts to turn it into information that can support an actual planting decision. Its approach combines: NASA-derived environmental context. Explainable, rule-based crop-rotation comparisons. Farmer-selected priorities and conditions. Offline-oriented planning. A lightweight interface for constrained devices. Optional AI explanations that remain separate from the decision engine. The project is designed to support farmers and agricultural extension workers, not replace local expertise. Technology used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the application. Node.js and serverless functions for optional backend services. Vercel for deployment. GitHub for source-code management. Hugging Face for the harmonized environmental dataset pipeline. Google Gemini API for optional AI-generated explanations. NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, MODIS NDVI, and SRTM for environmental data. Current limitations and next steps FieldShift is a working prototype, not a fully validated agricultural advisory system. The crop catalogue currently contains placeholder values that need to be replaced with sourced and expert-reviewed parameters. The climate information is zone-level rather than field-level. The experimental forecasting component needs rolling historical tests and comparison against baseline methods. Language translations need native-speaker review, and the Lite interface needs testing across actual feature-phone browsers. The next stage is to work with farmers, agricultural extension workers, agronomists, and language reviewers to validate the crop information, recommendations, forecasts, and real-world outcomes. The next step is not more AI. It is better local evidence. FieldShift NG aims to make climate-informed agricultural planning more accessible, transparent, and practical for smallholder farmers.
